title: Sensory Ataxia With Small Pupils / Recognise Late Neurosyphilis

blocks.text: Sensory Ataxia With Small Pupils / Recognise Late Neurosyphilis

Code R5-122 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, neurological examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 examining; at least 4 questioning) · UK hospital outpatient setting · Source dates listed in §15 · AMaC examiner-style educational station; not an official PACES marking scheme.
Please examine this patient’s lower limbs and relevant cranial nerves to investigate their unsteadiness. Present your findings and answer the examiners’ questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Sensory ataxia with areflexia and light–near dissociation raises tabes dorsalis. This is a pattern to recognise, not a diagnosis to announce without syphilis testing.
The Examiner Trap. Calling the gait “cerebellar” without testing proprioception misses the localisation; shaming the patient or skipping public-health and partner considerations neglects safety.

blocks.text: Not applicable — this is an examination encounter with a patient, not a communication or consultation role-player. The patient may answer brief, natural questions but is not a surrogate.
Patient setup: A 58-year-old with longstanding unsteadiness, worse in darkness, and intermittent shooting leg pain.
Finding-release protocol: do not announce a sign before the corresponding manoeuvre is performed.
Normal or mildly reduced limb power; absent ankle jerks and reduced knee jerks.
Marked impairment of toe joint position and vibration; positive Romberg and broad-based stamping gait.
Small, irregular pupils that accommodate on near fixation but respond poorly to direct light; no extensor plantars.
Normal-findings variant: If pupil findings are not present in a variant, report normal light and accommodation responses; tabes remains a differential based on other signs.
Examiner question ladder (4–6 questions; 4-minute discussion):
Q1 [R2]: What does Romberg mean here?  Model: Loss of proprioception: the patient compensates with vision; this is sensory ataxia.
Q2 [R3]: Explain the pupil finding.  Model: Accommodation preserved despite poor light reaction—light–near dissociation; not unique to syphilis.
Q3 [R4]: What confirms the cause?  Model: Syphilis serology, alongside specialist evaluation including CSF testing when neurological disease is suspected.
Q4 [R5]: How is neurosyphilis treated?  Model: Specialist-directed intravenous aqueous penicillin G according to CDC STI guidance; check allergy and follow-up.
Q5 [R6]: What other care is important?  Model: HIV testing, falls precautions, sexual-health discussion and partner notification support.

Curveball: The candidate states a diagnosis with certainty before discussing alternatives. Safe response: “These are findings and a leading differential; confirmation needs the appropriate investigation.”
[R1; Skill A] Examine power, reflexes, vibration, position sense, Romberg, gait and pupils.
[R2; Skill B] Identify sensory ataxia, absent reflexes and light–near dissociation.
[R3; Skill D] Suggest tabes dorsalis / neurosyphilis.
[R4; Skill E] Request syphilis serology, HIV test and specialist CSF assessment.
[R5; Skill E] Arrange urgent infectious disease or sexual-health consultation and guideline-based IV penicillin.
[R6; Skill G] Seek consent for eye assessment, guard against falls and discuss sensitive history privately.
[G] Gains consent, checks discomfort, and protects dignity during examination.

EXAMINER: “What is your impression?”

High-performance performance (adds prioritisation and anticipatory reasoning).
CANDIDATE: “Before examining, I will check whether any manoeuvre worsens pain or threatens balance and maintain your privacy.” [R6 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “Check direct light and near accommodation separately.” [R1 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “Which signs are discriminating?”
CANDIDATE: “Differentiate sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia. I will state clearly what I did not find.” [R2 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “What else could explain them?”
CANDIDATE: “Consider B12 deficiency, sensory neuropathy and other causes of light–near dissociation.” [R3 High-performance]
EXAMINER: “How does that change your plan?”
CANDIDATE: “Explain specialist evaluation for CNS involvement before treatment; address neurological rehabilitation, follow-up titres and partner services.” [R4 High-performance; R5 High-performance]
CANDIDATE: “I will document function and arrange appropriate assistance before the patient leaves.” [R6 High-performance]
Examiner note: Uses objective localisation, offers proportionate investigations, anticipates welfare concerns and avoids unjustified certainty.
R1 — Neurological sequence: Failing to examine power, reflexes, vibration, position sense, Romberg, gait and pupils makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R2 — Report objective findings: Failing to identify sensory ataxia, absent reflexes and light–near dissociation makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R3 — Diagnosis and differentials: Failing to suggest tabes dorsalis / neurosyphilis makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
R4 — Tests: Failing to request syphilis serology, HIV test and specialist CSF assessment makes the assessment less safe or less discriminating.
“The gait changes substantially when visual input is removed: this is sensory ataxia.”
“The pupil finding supports the hypothesis but is not diagnostic on its own.”
Sensory ataxia with areflexia and light–near dissociation raises tabes dorsalis. This is a pattern to recognise, not a diagnosis to announce without syphilis testing.
Calling the gait “cerebellar” without testing proprioception misses the localisation; shaming the patient or skipping public-health and partner considerations neglects safety.
Specialist-directed intravenous aqueous penicillin G according to CDC STI guidance; check allergy and follow-up.
THINK: prevent falls and treat neurological infection.
SAY: “Sensory ataxia with light–near dissociation.”
DO: Romberg with guarding; test pupils; arrange syphilis/HIV testing.
NUMBERS: CDC neurosyphilis guidance (2021) gives specialist IV therapy; no dose required for this encounter.
TRAP: light–near dissociation is not specific for syphilis.
FINISH: specialist assessment, antimicrobial care and confidential partner support.

CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Neurosyphilis (2021; website accessed 13 October 2026) — https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/neurosyphilis.htm — Supports: CSF assessment, IV penicillin treatment, HIV testing and follow-up. Access checked 13 October 2026.

CDC STI Treatment Guidelines: Syphilis (2021; website accessed 13 October 2026) — https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm — Supports: Tabes dorsalis as late neurosyphilis. Access checked 13 October 2026.
Educational use only. No automatic claim of examination scoring or independent clinical sign-off.

Distinguish loss of joint position and vibration sense with areflexia (sensory ataxia) from cerebellar ataxia. Confirm syphilis with appropriate treponemal and non-treponemal tests; suspected neurosyphilis requires specialist sexual-health/infectious-disease advice for CSF evaluation and appropriate penicillin-based therapy. Avoid treating a historical Argyll Robertson pupil pattern alone as diagnostic.
